articles.summary: Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with, regularly posted photos of herself with him on
articles.body: Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with, regularly posted photos of herself with him on WeChat. She also showed other pictures to customers as proof of her direct line to Nvidia’s boss. She even claimed Jensen would often celebrate her birthday with dinner and gifts, people familiar with her told The Information.That access, the report says, paid off. US officials have concluded that Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, and she allegedly helped move around 240,000 banned Nvidia chips into China, mostly H100 and H200 GPUs. A network of companies tied to her is estimated to have secured about $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI hardware during the three years she was in Jensen’s circle.Alice Huang used her photos with Jensen Huang as proof she could get Nvidia chipsAccording to The Information, Huang often pointed to her closeness with Nvidia and its suppliers as the reason she could always get AI chips. When shipments were delayed or stuck, she would allegedly step in and get them moving. An Nvidia China sales employee said she was a familiar face at the company’s annual event for local Chinese partners.The photos weren’t only on WeChat. The New York Times verified images from her social media showing the two together in Shanghai, at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters, at a golf resort south of San Jose and in Taiwan. Parker Schmitt, CEO of data software firm NetThunder, recalled a June 2024 night in Taipei when she told a group of executives, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here.” He turned up soon after and had a whiskey with them.A web of firms linked to Alice Huang bought $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia GPUsThe Information describes a “labyrinth” of companies built around Shanghai Century Litong, a data centre operator founded in June 2023. The shareholder that set it up was controlled by Huang Yu, Alice Huang’s sister. By October 2023, it had Nvidia Preferred Cloud Partner status, which comes with priority access to scarce chips. It went on to sell computing power to Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI labs.Megaspeed is the Singapore firm where Huang was a top executive. It was reportedly owned by a company carrying her Chinese name, Huang Le Limited, before being sold to the Singaporean entity Swiftdata. About $4.6 billion worth of AI chips came in through Megaspeed between 2023 and 2025, and another $2 billion went through its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. When US export officials inspected Speedmatrix’s data centres, much of the Nvidia hardware was still in boxes.The ties may go back further than people thought. The NYT reported that Huang met Jensen at an Italian restaurant in Singapore in December 2023. Four days after she restructured Megaspeed’s ownership, it was named an Nvidia cloud partner. A source also told The Information that Kang Wei, a fund manager introduced as her husband, met Jensen in the 2010s.Nvidia’s board is now investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with the suspected spyJensen, 63, admitted the affair on Sunday. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote in a memo to employees. “There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Nvidia’s board has opened an independent probe led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton and Joon H. Kim, a former acting US attorney. The board said it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Jensen stays on as CEO during the review.Nvidia has said it stopped all sales and shipments to Megaspeed in June 2025. Megaspeed says it is investigating the diversion claims internally. China has rejected the espionage allegations, and Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment.The NYT reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence about a year ago and took no action. On Monday, Trump said Jensen told him, “I had no idea that she was a spy,” and said he believes him. The Republican leaders of three House committees have asked Jensen to appear at a closed-door briefing this month. Those questions will land on a CEO who spent much of the past year pushing Washington to let Nvidia sell more freely to China.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Vice-President Jagdeep Dhankhar was taken to AIIMS hospital in New Delhi on Wednesday after he collapsed during his morning walk and briefly lost consciousness, news agency PTI reported citing sources.The 75-year-old was initially taken home by security personnel accompanying him in a police control room (PCR) vehicle.An ILBS medical team and AIIMS doctor attended to him and provided medical assistance. However, considering his health condition, he was later shifted to AIIMS in an ambulance.Dhankhar has been admitted to the hospital's cardio-neuro centre, where doctors from the cardiology department are conducting his medical evaluation and treatment. His health condition was not immediately known. AIIMS authorities have not issued an official statement so far.This is not the first time Dhankhar has experienced a medical emergency. In March 2025, he was admitted to AIIMS's critical care unit after complaining of chest pain and subsequently underwent angioplasty.He also fainted during the golden jubilee celebrations of Kumaon University in Nainital in June 2025. articles.title: Neil Patrick Harris hosted a New York gala that raised more than $2 million for animal protection, bringing together Vanessa Carlton, Amy Sedaris and Christie Brinkley as the group marked its work against animal testing
articles.summary: On a night of celebrity appearances, music and plant-based fine dining, animal welfare advocates gathered in New York City to support efforts to create a
articles.body: On a night of celebrity appearances, music and plant-based fine dining, animal welfare advocates gathered in New York City to support efforts to create a more compassionate world. Neil Patrick Harris hosted the annual To the Rescue! gala for Humane World for Animals, drawing in entertainment personalities, philanthropists and supporters to raise over $2 million for the organisation's work to protect animals and challenge cruelty across industries.A sparkling night for animal welfareAccording to online media reports, the event featured a special musical performance by Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter Vanessa Carlton, best known for her worldwide hit, “A Thousand Miles,” noted Humane World for Animals. Amy Sedaris, actress, author, and producer, longtime supporter of the gala and passionate rabbit advocate, was also in attendance for the evening.Supermodel Christie Brinkley was among the celebrities at the gathering. She presented the Corporate Conscience Award to Emulate, Inc. for its work developing technologies that can reduce reliance on animal testing, the online report adds.The company is involved in the development of human-relevant, animal-free research methods to achieve their scientific validation and acceptance in regulatory systems. Its work is part of a larger movement to change biomedical research with alternatives that may better mirror human biology, explains the Humane World for Animals website report.The gala was co-chaired by Georgina Bloomberg, Caren Fleit and Suzy Welch, as well as a leadership committee of philanthropists, business leaders and animal welfare advocates.Questioning the use of animal testingThe fundraising milestone comes as Humane World for Animals continues to expand its work to reduce the use of animals in scientific research and product testing. The organization, previously known as the Humane Society of the United States and Humane Society International, has been advocating for stronger protections and more ethical research practices for decades.Humane World for Animals’ strategy, according to the organization, includes legal action, scientific partnerships, public policy advocacy and regulatory engagement. Previous efforts have helped to end chimpanzee research and break down regulatory barriers that have long hindered the use of non-animal methods.Its current work also includes pushing major federal agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration, Environmental Protection Agency and National Institutes of Health to adopt more humane and human-relevant approaches.This change is important for the future of biomedical research, as advances in technology present opportunities for development of testing methods that do not use animals and improve relevance of scientific findings to human health.Plant-based dining elevates the eveningThe gala’s culinary experience also shone a light on sustainability. Guests enjoyed a cocktail reception and plant-based dinner curated by Overthrow Hospitality, a James Beard Award-nominated and Michelin-recognised restaurant group.Executive Chefs Amira Gharib and Haley Duren have designed a menu that reveals the creativity and potential of modern plant-based cooking.Other sponsors included Stray Dog, Liberty Mutual, TJX, Moroccanoil, Get Joy, Four Tails and Safeguard Global, as well as a host of organizations and businesses.From collective support to sustainable changeThe $2 million raised is more than just a successful fundraising night for Humane World for Animals. It offers support for campaigns addressing animal testing, cruelty and broader welfare challenges.The annual gathering seeks to harness public awareness and translate it into tangible action by uniting prominent figures from the realms of entertainment, business, and philanthropy to propel the movement toward a future characterized by greater compassion toward animals and where scientific advancement does not rely on their suffering.Images Courtesy: Charles Sykes and Angelina Katsanis / AP Images for Humane World for AnimalsYou use AI every day. articles.title: National Conference's twin troubles: Can Farooq Abdullah contain brewing revolt against Omar?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Two years after sweeping to power on a promise to reclaim Jammu and Kashmir’s political identity and dignity, Omar Abdullah’s government is
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Two years after sweeping to power on a promise to reclaim Jammu and Kashmir’s political identity and dignity, Omar Abdullah’s government is confronting the limits of governing a Union Territory with constrained powers.What began as a historic return to power in October 2024 has increasingly turned into a political and administrative tightrope. While 89-year-old National Conference patron Farooq Abdullah has stepped in to contain simmering discontent among MLAs left out of the cabinet expansion, an ideological rupture has emerged with the exit of Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, who has accused the party leadership of abandoning its core promises.Caught between disgruntled legislators seeking a greater share in government and a prominent party voice questioning its political compromises, the National Conference faces a twin challenge. The party has accused the BJP of exploiting its internal divisions to engineer an 'Operation Lotus' in Jammu and Kashmir. But is this an opposition attempt to destabilise the government, or does the turmoil point to a leadership crisis under Omar Abdullah?The show of unityThe gates of the Abdullahs' Gupkar residence in Srinagar opened to a familiar political spectacle last week as yet another party leadership put up a show of strength amid growing discontent within its ranks.Standing alongside 15 MLAs unhappy with the recent cabinet expansion, 89-year-old National Conference (NC) president Farooq Abdullah sought to project an image of an organisation firmly in control of its affairs."The baseless reports being spread that the National Conference is divided are completely false. This organisation is united, and those who think they can break this organisation should understand that it has never been broken and will never be broken," Farooq declared.He acknowledged that the legislators had genuine grievances and promised that some concerns would be addressed immediately, while others would be taken up gradually.But behind the show of unity, there's a bigger contradiction confronting Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah. The National Conference, which swept the 2024 assembly elections on the promise of reclaiming Kashmir's political identity, dignity and special status, is caught between the compromises of governing a Union Territory and the expectations of the constituency that brought it to power.The party is facing two distinct challenges. While a section of its MLAs is demanding a greater share in the government and a say in decision-making, one of its most prominent political voices, Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, has walked out accusing the leadership of abandoning the very promises on which it sought votes.The ideological rupture: Ruhullah's 'decree of freedom'The fragility of the NC's united front was exposed three days before Farooq met with the disgruntled legislators.On November 3, at a gathering in Behisht-e-Zehra Park in Budgam marking the 26th death anniversary of his assassinated father, Aga Syed Mehdi, Ruhullah announced his resignation from both the National Conference and the Lok Sabha.In an 80-minute address, the Srinagar MP launched a scathing attack on Farooq and Omar Abdullah, accusing the leadership of abandoning its promises on Article 370, political prisoners and public relief.Describing his departure as a "decree of freedom", Ruhullah called the NC a "deceitful, corrupt organisation"."You told people that you were the guardians of their dignity. You said that if anyone touched that dignity, it would be like grabbing you by the collar. That dignity was buried on August 5, 2019. Tell me now, where is that dignity? Where is that autonomy?" he asked, targeting the party leadership.He accused the NC of seeking power on promises it had failed to fulfil and said he could no longer lend his name to what he described as political humiliation.On November 6, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla formally accepted his resignation, creating a vacancy in the Srinagar parliamentary constituency.Ruhullah's departure is more than an organisational setback for the NC. Elected to the Lok Sabha on the party's ticket in 2024, he had emerged as one of its most vocal faces on the question of Kashmir's political rights after the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019.While Omar Abdullah has sought to pursue the restoration of statehood and special status through legislative and political channels, Ruhullah has demanded a more uncompromising approach. His exit gives him the opportunity to position himself as a voice of those who believe the NC has softened its stand after coming to power.He has hinted at launching a broader political movement rather than immediately forming a new party, saying he wants to bring together people committed to restoring the dignity and rights of Jammu and Kashmir.The NC, meanwhile, has questioned his own record, asking why he did not move a resolution or private member's bill in Parliament on special status or mobilise fellow MPs on the issue, despite having secured the support of more than 100 parliamentarians for an impeachment motion against an Allahabad High Court judge.The public exchange has exposed a larger ideological fault line: can the NC continue to claim ownership of the political struggle for Kashmir's rights while defending its record in government?The arithmetic ceilingWhile the ideological dissent has played out in public, the discontent within the legislative wing has centred on the distribution of power.The immediate trigger was the October 27 cabinet expansion, in which four new ministers were inducted, taking the council of ministers to its maximum permissible strength of nine.The restriction is rooted in Section 53 of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which caps the council of ministers at 10% of the total membership of the Legislative Assembly. With 90 elected seats, the permissible strength is nine, including the chief minister.This creates a structural constraint for Omar Abdullah. Unlike a full-fledged state, where the constitutional ceiling for the council of ministers is 15% of the assembly's strength, Jammu and Kashmir's Union Territory framework leaves the CM with a smaller pool of ministerial positions to distribute.With all nine positions occupied, accommodating more aspirants would require dropping or replacing existing ministers.Several senior legislators, including six-time MLA Mubarak Gul, were reportedly unhappy at being left out. The discontent was not limited to ministerial berths. The legislators also raised concerns about administrative functioning, organisational decisions and what they described as the concentration of authority among a small group of leaders and advisers.A group of 18 aggrieved legislators had met a week before the Friday meeting. The subsequent gathering of 15 MLAs at Gupkar brought their grievances directly to Farooq and Omar Abdullah.The legislators reportedly sought a review of the cabinet, changes in the functioning of the CM's office and a mechanism to ensure that elected representatives have a greater say in government decisions.One of the legislators, Nazir Gurezi, sought to play down speculation about the emergence of a separate faction."A few days ago, we sat together at a place, and from there, social media hyped it up as if a separate faction had emerged from the National Conference. No separate faction or party has emerged," he said.Gurezi added that the legislators had placed their concerns before the CM and the party president, who had assured them that the issues would be addressed.For Omar Abdullah, however, the problem is not merely placating a group of unhappy MLAs. The cabinet expansion has exhausted the government's primary instrument of political accommodation. Any reshuffle could create fresh resentment among those who have already secured ministerial positions.Farooq's intervention may have prevented the discontent from turning into an open confrontation for now, but the leadership will have to find ways of accommodating senior legislators without triggering another round of dissatisfaction.Omar Abdullah's Union Territory dilemmaThe constraints facing Omar Abdullah go beyond cabinet arithmetic. They strike at the heart of the political contradiction of running an elected government in a Union Territory where the Lieutenant Governor and the Centre retain significant powers.Omar has repeatedly complained about the limits placed on his government, particularly in matters involving administration and the functioning of the bureaucracy.During the September 2026 assembly proceedings on a resolution seeking immediate restoration of full statehood, he revealed that the Law Secretary had written to the Speaker questioning whether the resolution should be discussed because the matter was sub judice. The chief secretary had also written to the Speaker.Omar, who also holds the law portfolio, expressed surprise at the communications."I am a law minister and I don't know that my law secretary is giving you an opinion. As a CM I don't know the chief secretary is writing to the Speaker against my resolution. I don't know on whose behalf it is being done," he said.He went on to question whether such a situation would arise in a full-fledged state."Would you think such a thing would happen in any State? This happens only in UT where a CM moves a resolution and the law secretary gives an opinion against it," he said.The episode illustrates the difficult position in which the chief minister finds himself. To deliver on everyday governance, including infrastructure, electricity, welfare schemes and administrative decisions, Omar has to work within the existing institutional arrangement. But the same arrangement limits his authority and has become a source of political frustration for his government.Every compromise with the Centre risks being interpreted by sections of the electorate as a dilution of the NC's political promises. Every confrontation, meanwhile, can further constrain the government's ability to function.The NC's August 19, 2024 manifesto had made restoration of Articles 370 and 35A a key promise. It also pledged to work towards restoration of statehood, repeal of the Public Safety Act and release of political prisoners.The party subsequently sought to demonstrate its commitment through the assembly. On November 6, 2024, the House passed a resolution seeking restoration of special status, a move Ruhullah had initially welcomed.But two years after the abrogation of Article 370, the Centre has given no indication of reversing its decision. Statehood, too, remains unresolved, while the reservation policy has become another source of friction between the government and sections of the electorate.The NC has defended its record on reservations, saying its cabinet sub-committee has initiated changes but that the decisions are awaiting action from the Centre and the Lieutenant Governor's administration.Farooq Abdullah, after Friday's meeting, reiterated that the party would continue its fight for statehood and Articles 370 and 35A, taking the struggle to its "logical conclusion".Political space opening up beyond NCRuhullah's exit could challenge the NC's claim to represent Kashmir's political aspirations. Having been elected on its ticket in 2024, he may now seek to occupy the political space he believes the party has vacated.The political implications will depend on whether Ruhullah can translate his criticism into an organised platform and attract support beyond his existing constituency. His resignation has already created a vacancy in Srinagar, and the eventual by-election could become an important test of the political space he hopes to occupy.The BJP has been quick to seize on the National Conference's internal troubles. On November 3, BJP national vice president Ram Madhav said Ruhullah's rally in Budgam had the blessings of "our people". The NC subsequently accused the BJP of attempting "Operation Lotus" in Kashmir, a charge the party has denied. For the BJP, the public friction within the ruling party offers an opportunity to question its cohesion and, more importantly, Omar Abdullah's leadership.The Congress, the NC's alliance partner, has taken a more cautious line. It has sought to play down the developments, attributing Ruhullah's departure to ideological differences while expressing confidence that the NC would resolve its internal disagreements. But the strains within its ally also pose a political concern for the Congress, given its investment in the governing arrangement.For the Abdullahs, however, the challenge is that the two crises have unfolded back-to-back on different fronts.Farooq Abdullah's show of unity at Gupkar may have helped contain the immediate optics of the MLAs' rebellion. It does little, however, to answer the larger questions raised by Ruhullah's exit.The next few months will answer whether Omar Abdullah can hold his flock together and retain the public's trust at the same time.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Washington mother lost her three children in a 2017 crash, then her husband had to sue her after an insurance dispute; an appeals court has now erased $47 million in punitive damages but upheld other awards
articles.summary: A Washington State appeals court has removed about $47 million in punitive and additional statutory damages awarded against Nationwide Affinity Insurance
articles.body: A Washington State appeals court has removed about $47 million in punitive and additional statutory damages awarded against Nationwide Affinity Insurance Company. However, it upheld key findings that the insurer acted in bad faith when handling a tragic car crash in 2017. The decision by Division III of the Washington Court of Appeals, published on 10 November 2026, is the latest development in a long-running legal case. The case began after a crash that killed three young children and seriously injured their parents. The case involved Meseret Shiferaw, whose vehicle was hit by a semi-truck during a trip to Alberta, Canada, in 2017. All three of her children died in the crash. Shiferaw suffered a broken back, while her husband, Solomon Agere, broke his neck.Tragic crash and legal complicationsAfter the crash, the family faced complicated legal and insurance disputes over their coverage. Shiferaw had a personal car insurance policy with Nationwide. Under the rules for accidents outside the state, the policy provided up to $200,000 in liability coverage. Nationwide initially refused to pay the full policy limit directly to Agere unless he agreed to a complete release of all possible third-party claims. These included potential claims against the truck driver involved in the crash. Because the insurer did not agree to settle the claims between family members immediately, Agere took legal action against his wife. He wanted to establish her legal responsibility and secure payment from the insurance policy. In early 2020, the Spokane County Superior Court ordered Nationwide to pay Agere the full $200,000 liability limit. Agere and Shiferaw later went through arbitration. The process found that Agere's third-party damages were worth more than $17 million. Shiferaw then filed her own claims against Nationwide. She argued that the insurer had acted in bad faith, failed in its duty to handle the claims properly, and broken Washington State insurance rules.Trial court awards tens of millionsDuring the trial at Spokane County Superior Court, a jury reached a large verdict against Nationwide. It found that the insurer had acted in bad faith and had been negligent when handling the claims. The trial court awarded Shiferaw $27.136 million in compensation. This included $136,000 for financial losses and $27 million for emotional and other non-financial harm. The trial court also used legal rules about which state's laws should apply. It decided that Ohio law could be used to award punitive damages because Nationwide is based in that state. This resulted in an additional punitive damages award. The court also applied a legal multiplier under Washington's Insurance Fair Conduct Act (IFCA). This increased the total amount Nationwide was ordered to pay to more than $74 million. Nationwide appealed the decision. The company challenged the IFCA claim, the use of Ohio law to award punitive damages for a case outside the state, and the overall amount of damages.Appeals court strikes down punitive damagesWriting on behalf of the three-judge appeals panel, Judge Murphy upheld some parts of the lower court's decision but overturned others. The Court of Appeals found that the trial court was wrong to use Ohio common law to award punitive damages. Under Washington State law, punitive damages are generally not allowed unless a specific law clearly permits them. The appeals panel decided that Washington law applied to the legal claims in this case. As a result, the multi-million-dollar punitive damages award was removed. The appeals court also overturned the finding that Nationwide was liable under the Insurance Fair Conduct Act. The judges explained that IFCA covers first-party insurance claims, such as personal injury protection or uninsured motorist benefits. It does not cover disputes involving third-party liability insurance. Removing the IFCA claim also removed the additional amount calculated under the law's statutory multiplier. This wiped out another major part of the original judgment.Primary bad faith ruling upheldAlthough the appeals court removed the punitive damages and statutory increases, it kept the jury's main finding that Nationwide acted in bad faith and was negligent under common law. The court also upheld the main compensation awarded to Shiferaw for the insurer's bad faith and negligence. This means the family will still receive millions of dollars in compensation. Lawyers representing Shiferaw, including the Luvera Law Firm, had previously said that money recovered through the case would help support an educational foundation. The family created the foundation in memory of their three children. The appeals court's decision reduces the judgment to the main compensation amount while rejecting Shiferaw's separate appeal for an injunction under the Consumer Protection Act. Neither side has publicly confirmed whether it plans to ask the Washington Supreme Court to review the decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A tech executive paid a couple $97,000 under a confidential settlement; after the woman contacted his employers and posted assault allegations, an appeals court upheld $2.75 million in damages awarded to him
articles.summary: A senior technology executive has won a $2.75 million damages award (approximately £2.1 million) after a US appeals court upheld a ruling against a woman
articles.body: A senior technology executive has won a $2.75 million damages award (approximately £2.1 million) after a US appeals court upheld a ruling against a woman who publicly accused him of assault after accepting money in a confidential settlement. The case of Michael Fitzgerald, et al v. Ronda McNae was decided on November 10, 2026. The ruling highlights the legal consequences of breaking confidentiality agreements, particularly when a court finds that someone deliberately breached the terms and caused harm to another person's career and reputation. According to the opinion published by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, the dispute began with a confidential settlement agreement. Under the deal, Michael Fitzgerald, a technology executive, paid Ronda McNae $97,000 (approximately £79,000) to settle earlier disputes. Both sides also agreed to keep the agreement and its details private.Confidentiality agreement breachedDespite accepting the payment, McNae later began sharing information that the court found violated the agreement. The Eleventh Circuit's ruling explained that McNae contacted Fitzgerald's employers and other professional contacts. She also made serious accusations against him, including claims of rape and sexual assault. McNae also posted the accusations on social media and other public websites. Fitzgerald and a second plaintiff, Yelany de Varona, argued that her actions were intended to damage his career, reputation and ability to earn a living. They said these actions directly broke the promises McNae had made in the settlement agreement. According to the court records, Fitzgerald filed a lawsuit against McNae in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida. He sought compensation for the financial and personal harm caused by the alleged breaches.Lower court finds for executiveThe lower court initially ruled in Fitzgerald's favour. It found that McNae had broken the clear and legally binding terms of the confidential settlement agreement. The district court granted summary judgment to Fitzgerald on his breach-of-contract claim. It found that a valid agreement existed, that McNae had seriously violated its terms and that Fitzgerald was entitled to damages. The court then held a separate trial to decide how much compensation he should receive. It awarded Fitzgerald a total of $2,746,703.27 in economic and non-economic damages. The ruling did not uphold separate claims for defamation or intentional infliction of emotional distress. These claims had been dismissed earlier in the case.Breakdown of massive damages awardThe damages upheld by the appeals court included both financial losses and compensation for harm to Fitzgerald's reputation. The total award was $2,746,703.27, rather than a punitive damages award. The Eleventh Circuit's opinion explained that Fitzgerald received $2 million in non-economic damages because of the damage to his professional reputation. The lower court found clear evidence that he had built a strong reputation and performed well at SoftwareONE before McNae broke the agreement. The court also found that McNae deliberately broke the agreement to damage his reputation. It estimated that Fitzgerald would need five to six years to rebuild his professional standing and would lose $2 million in salary and bonuses during that period. The remaining $746,703.27 covered economic losses. This included the original $97,000 settlement payment, $274,453.27 in long-term incentives, $219,300 in lost bonuses and $155,950 in lost performance share units. The court also considered evidence that Fitzgerald had earned £550,000 a year before the dispute. He had been expected to become the CEO of a new company, but following the breach, he was placed on paid leave and could no longer work or communicate with colleagues, customers and business partners.Appeals court reaffirms decisionIn her appeal to the Eleventh Circuit, Ronda McNae asked the court to overturn or reduce the multi-million-dollar award. Her legal team argued that the amount was excessive and that the lower court had made errors when deciding the case. However, the three-judge appeals panel rejected her arguments and upheld the lower court's decision. The Eleventh Circuit found no clear error in the damages calculation and concluded that the evidence supported the amount awarded to Fitzgerald. The panel noted that the lower court had carefully considered the financial and professional harm caused by McNae's actions. It also reviewed evidence from expert witness Sheri Fiske, who calculated that the agreement breaches had caused $472,250 in economic losses. Documents from Fitzgerald's employer also supported the evidence presented during the trial. The appeals court concluded that the district court had properly calculated both the economic and non-economic damages. It found no reason to overturn the $2,746,703.27 judgment. The decision, dated November 10, 2026, leaves the full damages award in place and confirms that Fitzgerald is entitled to the compensation ordered by the lower court.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 11-year-old non-verbal boy with autism was sued by a San Jose neighbour who called his noises a public nuisance; three years later, a jury has awarded his family $8 million for emotional distress
articles.summary: A family in San Jose, California, has won an $8 million jury award after a prolonged legal dispute with a neighbour who took issue with the sounds their
articles.body: A family in San Jose, California, has won an $8 million jury award after a prolonged legal dispute with a neighbour who took issue with the sounds their autistic child made while playing in the backyard. According to reporting by KRON4 and NBC Bay Area, the dispute began when the neighbour filed a lawsuit against the family, arguing that the child's vocalisations amounted to a public nuisance. The family's subsequent countersuit resulted in a jury verdict in their favour. The boy, identified as Ezekiel Arvayo, was 11 when the original dispute became a legal matter. He has Level 3 autism, is non-verbal and requires extensive daily support. He is now 14, according to NBC Bay Area's October 2026 report.How the dispute beganThe family was living in a rented house on Boynton Avenue with Ezekiel's grandfather when their next-door neighbour initiated legal proceedings in December 2023. She sought a court order to address what she considered a public nuisance and also requested restrictions on the family's conduct.The neighbour alleged that the child frequently made loud noises in the backyard, disrupting her ability to work from home. She also claimed that the situation had affected her professional life and prevented her from enjoying her property. The family disputed these allegations. In March 2024, Serena filed a cross-complaint, explaining that her son's vocalisations were linked to his autism and were not deliberate attempts to disturb anyone.According to the family's legal filing, Ezekiel requires constant supervision because of his communication and sensory difficulties. He attends school and behavioural therapy during weekdays, while spending some of his time at home playing outdoors. One of his favourite activities is chasing bubbles in the backyard, which sometimes prompts him to express excitement through vocal stimming, a form of self-stimulatory behaviour.Family alleges neighbour's remarks caused distressThe family's cross-complaint also detailed an earlier interaction between Serena and the neighbour, before the dispute reached court. According to the filing, the neighbour had approached Serena and asked her to stop allowing Ezekiel to play in the backyard because of the noises he made. When Serena attempted to explain her son's condition and his inability to communicate verbally, the neighbour allegedly questioned whether his autism could be cured.The family also alleged that the neighbour contacted their landlord through text messages to complain about the sounds coming from the property. The allegations formed part of the family's case that the neighbour's actions had caused them considerable emotional distress. These details were presented in the family's legal filings and were not independently established as separate findings by the jury.Jury awards family $8 millionThe neighbour's original public nuisance lawsuit was dismissed in September 2026. The family's countersuit subsequently went before a jury in Santa Clara County, which awarded them $8 million for intentional infliction of emotional distress, according to reports by KRON4 and NBC Bay Area.The verdict was welcomed by the family's legal representatives, who said the proceedings had been a lengthy and difficult experience. The lawyers also said the compensation would help provide Ezekiel with the assistance and security he would need in the future. The neighbour's attorney had not immediately responded to media requests for comment, according to KRON4.The legal dispute also had consequences for the family's living arrangements. Serena and her son eventually moved out of the Boynton Avenue rental property, reportedly taking on higher housing costs at their new residence. In an interview with NBC Bay Area, Serena said the most important outcome was that her son had been treated with dignity. She also expressed hope that the case would encourage greater understanding and compassion towards children with autism and their families.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2019, Tiffany Haddish founded a charity inspired by her years in foster care, when she carried her belongings in trash bags; it now distributes more than 2,000 suitcases annually to foster youth
articles.summary: American comedian Tiffany Haddish has turned her difficult childhood experiences in the foster care system into a major charity project.
articles.body: American comedian Tiffany Haddish has turned her difficult childhood experiences in the foster care system into a major charity project. Her foundation now gives thousands of suitcases to children facing similar challenges across the United States every year. The project began in 2019 and was inspired by Haddish's own experiences moving between foster homes. Since then, it has grown into an effort to give young people more dignity and comfort during difficult changes in their lives. According to the She Ready Foundation, the organisation now gives away more than 2,000 suitcases and other pieces of luggage to foster children every year. The goal is to stop children from having to carry their belongings in plastic rubbish bags.Turning trash bags into travel dignityThe suitcase programme comes directly from Haddish's own childhood experiences, which she has often discussed in interviews and publications. She spent several years in foster care and was often moved from one home to another with little warning. Because she did not have proper luggage, her belongings were packed into black plastic rubbish bags. She has described this experience as deeply upsetting and humiliating. In her 2017 memoir, The Last Black Unicorn, Haddish wrote about how these experiences made her feel worthless. The book shares several details about her childhood. Later interviews, including those reported by People magazine, also highlighted this painful memory. In one widely reported conversation, she recalled being told to "only take what you can fit in this black trash bag". She understood this as a message that "you don’t belong, you’re just garbage". Learning that children still face this treatment today inspired Haddish to create the foundation's luggage programme. Data from the US government's Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System (AFCARS) shows that children in foster care can move between several homes while in the system. Each move creates another challenge, as children must pack and carry their personal belongings.Partnerships enable large-scale impactThe She Ready Foundation understands that one person cannot solve such a widespread problem alone. That is why the charity works with major manufacturers and retailers to support its work. According to details shared on shereadyfoundation.org, partnerships with well-known brands such as Samsonite and Away have played an important role in the success of the luggage programme. These partnerships help the foundation obtain strong, good-quality suitcases that can be given to children in foster care. The organisation explains on its website that the aim is not simply to provide bags, but to make sure every child has "their very own" piece of luggage. Having a suitcase of their own can give children a sense of stability and personal space during an uncertain time in their lives. Through these partnerships and other efforts, the foundation says it now provides more than 2,000 foster children with proper suitcases every year. This is a major expansion of the small project Haddish first imagined.Foundation extends its reach beyond luggageAlthough providing suitcases remains an important part of its work, the She Ready Foundation has expanded its support to other areas of young people's lives. According to a recent foundation update, the organisation now offers programmes that help foster youth develop skills, find mentors and explore career opportunities. Information published on shereadyfoundation.org on 19 October 2026 about its Summer Cohort programme explains these wider efforts. During the summer, the foundation ran a mentorship programme for current and former foster youth. It offered guidance, support and useful resources, with a focus on education and career development. The programme ended with a public event where participants could present what they had achieved. One of the programme's major achievements was the premiere of a film called Time’s Up, which was produced by young people and shown in Toronto. The foundation explained that the project gave participants practical experience in film production and event management. It also showed how the right support can help young people develop their creative abilities and prepare for future careers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A widow clearing out her late husband's shed found a biscuit tin packed with 62 gold coins, including pieces he bought for £70 to £80 each in 1975; after 50 years hidden away, the collection sold for £113,000
articles.summary: A metal biscuit tin that had been forgotten in a garden shed near Penzance, Cornwall, has sold for £113,000 at auction.
articles.body: A metal biscuit tin that had been forgotten in a garden shed near Penzance, Cornwall, has sold for £113,000 at auction. The tin contained 62 gold coins that had been collected and stored away around 50 years ago. The unexpected discovery happened when a widow began clearing out the buildings belonging to her late husband. She took the dusty tin to Lay’s Auctioneers to find out what was inside.Uncovering a hidden fortune in PenzanceThe shed clearance seemed like an ordinary task until the tin was brought to staff at Lay's Auctioneers in Cornwall. At first, the container appeared to hold everyday household items, along with a few loose silver coins on top. However, when auction experts looked more closely, they found dozens of gold coins hidden beneath the other items. Many of them were still inside their original mint packaging.The collection included 41 South African Krugerrand gold coins and 21 British gold sovereigns. Speaking to The Independent, a representative from the auction house described the surprise of finding the coins. "I plonked it down and looked inside and saw silver coins," the spokesman said. "It was just astonishing. We have had discoveries before but all that gold was just remarkable".A mid-1970s investment left forgottenThe late owner had quietly bought the gold coins in 1975, during a period of economic difficulties in the United Kingdom. He paid between £70 and £80 for each coin. However, he never told his family about the investment. Instead, he placed the coins in the shed, where they remained untouched for around 50 years. "Our client didn't know that her husband had just gone and spent a few thousand pounds on this gold investment and stashed it away and didn't tell her," a representative for Nationwide Coins said in a review of the sale.When the coins were bought in 1975, gold was worth much less than it is today. Over the next 50 years, gold prices increased sharply around the world. This turned what had started as a small investment into a valuable collection worth a large amount of money. "The price of gold is astronomical at the moment so it was an amazing investment by this man," a spokesperson for Lay's Auctioneers told The Independent. "What a shrewd chap her husband was".Competitive bidding drives total past estimatesLay's Auctioneers prepared the collection for sale and attracted interest from coin collectors and gold investors across the UK. With gold prices already high, buyers competed for the coins. Every lot from the biscuit tin collection was sold, taking the total auction price beyond £113,000. The money from the sale has now been handed to the widow. The discovery brought an end to a 50-year investment story that began with a quiet purchase of gold coins for just £70 in 1975.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK PM Burnham vows to unveil 10-year plan for Britain before Christmas amid Badenoch's vision jibe
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announces a strategic 10-year plan for Britain to be unveiled before the Christmas recess, amidst criticisms from Tory leader Kemi Badenoch regarding his vision and reliance on consultants.
articles.body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed that his Government's 10-year plan for Britain will be presented to Parliament before the Christmas recess, setting a deadline for a strategy that has faced questions over its ambition and the policies it will deliver.Speaking during Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs), Burnham said the document would provide the country with long-term leadership and stability. His announcement also marked a shift from his earlier suggestion that the timetable could extend into next year.“We will present our plan for Britain to this House before it rises for the Christmas recess,” Burnham told MPs.His commitment came after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch questioned whether the Prime Minister had a clear vision for the country and challenged his reliance on external consultants to develop the strategy.Badenoch said Burnham had entered Downing Street promising to reverse 40 years of neoliberalism, but asked whether he needed Boston Consulting Group to write the plan because he lacked a vision of his own.“Is it really true he has so little vision for this country he needs the Boston Consulting Group to write it for him?” she asked.Burnham did not deny working with the consultancy. He defended the need for a long-term strategy, saying his aim was to provide the stability that the previous administration had failed to deliver.“I am determined to give the leadership that this country needs,” he said.Badenoch also criticised last month's Budget, describing it as a “do-nothing Budget” and accusing the Government of postponing major decisions, including those concerning defence funding, until the spending review. She said there was still no clarity on when that review would take place.The 10-year plan has been used to explain why several policy decisions were not addressed in the Budget. The document is expected to outline Burnham's plans to transfer more powers to local leaders across the UK and reform the social care system.However, it is not expected to set out a route towards increasing defence spending to 3% of gross domestic product by 2030. That decision has been deferred to a spending review expected in the second half of the year.There are also questions over whether the strategy will include measures relating to benefits. Louise Haigh, the Prime Minister's de facto deputy, declined to confirm last week whether the issue would feature in the plan.Burnham said the strategy would include a “compelling” vision for reindustrialisation, but Labour MPs representing areas with a history of industrial decline have raised concerns about the Government's approach.Members of the Reindustrialisation Research Group (RRG), made up largely of MPs from Red Wall constituencies, want stronger action to support heavy industries facing rising energy costs.A delegation from the group is expected to meet Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson to discuss its concerns and press the Government for more concrete proposals.Andy MacNae, head of the RRG, told The Guardian that the Government's reindustrialisation strategy still had significant gaps that needed to be addressed.“The ten-year plan is a chance to fill them, but in the briefings we have been given that is not what we are seeing,” he said.MacNae acknowledged that ministers had engaged with the group but said MPs were still waiting for more constructive measures. He warned that the country risked continuing to lose industrial capacity rather than rebuilding it.“The risk is we don't see reindustrialisation at all, and continue to see deindustrialisation,” he said.Jonathan Hinder, an RRG member and MP for Pendle and Clitheroe, also called for more decisive action, arguing that the Government needed to move beyond broad commitments.“Making reindustrialisation cannot just be about political slogans,” Hinder said.“We are going in the wrong direction and we need pretty drastic action, but we are not yet seeing that from this government.”You use AI every day. articles.body: Anthropic is stepping up its efforts to use artificial intelligence (AI) to accelerate drug discovery, working with biotechnology companies to develop potential treatments for cancer, food allergies and rare diseases.The company behind AI chatbot Claude said it has partnered with six organisations, including Bristol Myers Squibb, Generate Biomedicines and BigHat Biosciences, to explore how AI can speed up different stages of developing new medicines.The announcement comes amid growing interest in the use of AI to identify potential drugs, design molecules and reduce the time and cost involved in medical research.AI helps develop potential cancer treatmentsOne of the projects involves Generate Biomedicines, which is working to adapt CAR T-cell therapy, traditionally used against blood cancers, to treat solid tumours.Using Claude Code, six scientists from Generate proposed a redesigned version of a section of the therapy's genetic instructions. The new design was about 70 per cent shorter than the standard version.Laboratory tests found that it helped immune cells produce roughly 10 times more receptors, improved their ability to kill tumour cells and allowed them to remain active for longer.Another collaboration with BigHat Biosciences focused on improving two potential drug candidates, including one designed to target cancer cells. After testing around 1,010 variations, researchers found that the best version bound to its target more than 10 times as tightly as the original.AI takes on drug discovery and researchAnthropic also said its collaboration with Divergence Labs generated around 35,000 antibody designs in approximately a month to develop a potential treatment for food allergies.Separately, its work with Enveda helped reduce the time required for human review of manufacturing documents by 89 per cent.Anthropic has also started its own drug discovery programmes, including research into rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy.However, the company cautioned that much of this research remains at the preclinical stage, meaning the potential treatments have not yet reached human trials.It said one of its muscular dystrophy drug candidates could be ready to enter human clinical trials as early as late 2028, provided the promising results continue to hold up.You use AI every day. articles.title: University of Michigan Police Department's $127,500 Flock Safety deal for 15 AI cameras exposed; never installed, law professor and students raise surveillance and privacy concerns
articles.summary: The University of Michigan Police Department (UMPD) signed a $127,500 contract with surveillance technology company Flock Safety to acquire automated
articles.body: The University of Michigan Police Department (UMPD) signed a $127,500 contract with surveillance technology company Flock Safety to acquire automated licence plate reader cameras, but the equipment was never installed or put into use, according to records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. The revelation has raised fresh questions about the university's surveillance plans, data privacy and the growing use of automated monitoring technology on American campuses.According to a report by The Michigan Daily, the agreement was signed on February 3, 2025, by Jennifer Carr, a University of Michigan procurement agent, on behalf of the police department. Mark Smith, Flock Safety's general counsel, signed the contract for the company. The agreement was not publicly announced at the time.UMPD later confirmed that the 15 cameras covered under the deal were neither installed nor operational.What did the University of Michigan's $127,500 Flock Safety deal include?Under the agreement, the university committed to paying $63,750 annually, amounting to $127,500 over an initial 24-month period. The contract covered 15 Falcon Flex cameras, described as law-enforcement-grade tactical deployment equipment, along with FlockOS Essentials software, Vehicle Fingerprint artificial intelligence technology and 15 battery packs.However, it remains unclear whether the university ever made the payment.Unlike conventional security cameras, automated licence plate readers scan passing vehicles and compare their registration numbers against databases containing information about stolen vehicles, outstanding warrants and other law enforcement watchlists.The technology also records details such as a vehicle's make, model, colour, distinguishing features, bumper stickers, roof racks and visible damage. This information can be used to build a searchable record of where a vehicle has travelled over time.The Falcon Flex cameras covered under the agreement were designed to capture vehicles from the rear. They were not intended to monitor pedestrians, sidewalks or intersections.Cameras could have enabled extensive vehicle tracking and data sharingOne of the key concerns surrounding the agreement is the extent of surveillance and data-sharing capabilities offered by Flock's technology.The contract allowed the cameras to be used for any "legitimate public safety and/or business purpose", including the "prevention of commercial harm", as outlined in Section 1.14. It did not specify where the 15 cameras were supposed to be installed.The agreement also included provisions for data retention and sharing. Under its terms, information collected by the cameras would automatically be deleted after 30 days unless UMPD manually archived it. However, Flock has since reduced its company-wide default data retention period to seven days.Another provision, Section 5.3, allowed Flock to disclose footage to law enforcement agencies, government officials or third parties without a warrant if the company had a "good faith belief" that such disclosure was legally necessary.The FlockOS platform also offered access to statewide and nationwide searches, along with a Community Network comprising privately owned cameras. Although it remains unclear whether UMPD ever activated these features, the agreement could have allowed the department to search vehicle registration numbers across participating Flock camera networks.The arrangement also involved reciprocal access, meaning other participating government, law enforcement and private agencies could potentially have searched data captured by UMPD's 15 cameras.University expands campus surveillance amid concerns over privacyThe Flock Safety agreement came at a time when the University of Michigan was making significant changes to its campus security infrastructure.During the summer of 2025, the university's Division of Public Safety and Security installed surveillance cameras at the entrances of most campus buildings, as well as in the Law Quad and the Diag.The expansion prompted concerns among some members of the university community, particularly against the backdrop of pro-Palestine protests during the 2024-2025 academic year, which were met with force by UMPD.In the autumn of 2025, the university formally launched the Security Technology Enhancement Project, a large-scale initiative aimed at modernising physical security and emergency communication infrastructure across all three campuses.Around the same period, the university revised its institutional policies, removing explicit restrictions on the use of surveillance cameras and eliminating requirements for a student and faculty security oversight committee. The Michigan Daily also reported that the committee appeared not to have been meeting as required.These developments have raised questions about the extent of surveillance on campus and the safeguards available to protect students' privacy.Law professor and students raise concerns over surveillanceLaw professor Michael Steinberg expressed concern that the growing use of surveillance technology could fundamentally change how security is maintained on campus."The major issue is that we've moved from investigating suspects to collecting information about everyone," Steinberg said.He added that he feared the University of Michigan was moving towards a system in which campus-wide surveillance could become the norm.LSA senior Radha Tanner, co-chair of the American Civil Liberties Union at the university, also questioned the potential misuse of Flock's data-sharing capabilities."It's not the issue of the cameras as they are, but more so how they are being used and by who to do what," Tanner said.She further argued that the technology's lack of adequate regulation could leave room for misuse and exploitation, extending its applications beyond legitimate law enforcement requirements such as tracking stolen vehicles or assisting in missing persons investigations.What has the University of Michigan said about the Flock Safety contract?Responding to questions from The Michigan Daily, UMPD deputy chief of police Melissa Overton said the department selected Flock Safety to address public safety requirements and investigative needs."UMPD selected Flock Safety as a tool to support legitimate public safety and investigative needs; the acquisition was not prompted by any single specific security concern," Overton wrote in an email.She also clarified that the agreement had gone through the university's procurement and contracting procedures and did not require approval from the Board of Regents or a separate public approval process.Importantly, Overton confirmed that the cameras had never been installed or activated."The 15 Falcon Flex cameras referenced in the agreement are not currently installed or in use," she wrote.However, she did not explain why the university ultimately decided against installing the equipment or when that decision was made.Flock Safety faces wider scrutiny over surveillance technologyThe controversy surrounding the University of Michigan's agreement comes amid a broader national debate in the United States over automated licence plate readers and the growing use of surveillance technology.Flock Safety has faced increasing scrutiny over concerns about data-sharing practices, privacy safeguards and the possibility of information being accessed or used beyond its original public safety purpose.Lawmakers in Michigan from both political parties have also called for tighter regulations governing Flock cameras.While the University of Michigan maintains that its 15-camera agreement remains unused, the contract has brought attention to the extent of surveillance capabilities it had agreed to procure, including access to wider networks of cameras and vehicle movement data.The episode has also raised a larger question about the balance between campus security and individual privacy, particularly when surveillance systems have the potential to collect information on people who are not suspected of any wrongdoing.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Two Special Police Officers (SPOs) went missing from Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district on Wednesday, prompting a search operation, officials said, according to news agency PTI.Both officers were part of the Special Operations Group (SOG) deployed in the Kiyar area of Dachhan in Kishtwar.According to reports, the two SPOs had left for patrol duty earlier in the day. Police teams have launched a search operation to trace them, officials said, PTI reported.The incident comes amid a separate attack on security personnel in Kulgam district, where three Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel were injured after unidentified motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire at a security checkpoint on Wednesday afternoon.The firing took place at around 2.15 pm when the assailants targeted CRPF personnel deployed at a naka, or security checkpoint, in Kulgam, the force said. The attackers fled shortly after opening fire."There has been firing on CRPF Naka at Kulgam, Kashmir. Three personnel injured. Operations are going on to nab the perpetrators and best possible treatment is being provided to the injured personnel," the CRPF said in a statement.The injured personnel were shifted to Government Medical College (GMC), Anantnag, for treatment. Security agencies have launched a search operation to track down the attackers, an official said.The checkpoint is around 4 km from the National Highway. Of the three injured personnel, two sustained minor injuries, while the third was reported to be slightly serious, the official said, ANI reported.The injured CRPF personnel have been identified as Head Constable Somveer Singh and Constables Rakesh Dass and Santosh Chandru. Chandru, a resident of West Bengal, sustained injuries to his abdomen and spine. His condition was stated to be slightly serious.Dass, who hails from Assam, suffered a bullet injury to his leg, while Singh, a resident of Madhya Pradesh, sustained a bullet injury to his arm. articles.body: Cuttack: President Droupadi Murmu will inaugurate the historic maritime fair, Baliyatra, on Nov 24 on the banks of river Mahanadi in Cuttack, said the district administration, adding a special security and traffic management plan has been chalked. Chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi and Governor Braj Mohan Ram are also scheduled to be present on the occasion.The eight-day maritime festival, which will continue till Dec 1, will be organised across both the upper and lower Baliyatra grounds this year.The administration has completed the land allocation process for more than 500 plots, while further formalities are underway.“President Murmu has graciously consented to inaugurate the historic Baliyatra. A citywide beautification drive will also be undertaken ahead of the event. All departments are working in coordination to ensure a smooth and memorable inauguration,” said a district administration official.The district administration and Cuttack Municipal Corporation's citywide beautification drive will focus on road repairs, lighting and removal of encroachments.A senior district administration official said greater emphasis will be laid on cleanliness, safe drinking water, additional temporary toilets, uninterrupted power supply, food safety and medical facilities on the fairgrounds. Adequate lighting will also be ensured across the grounds and surrounding areas, said the senior official.Meanwhile, the theme for this year's 'Cuttack in Cuttack' initiative will be finalised based on suggestions and opinions received from the public, the administration said.Cultural programmes and competitions will be organised alongside the fair, which attracts lakhs of visitors from Odisha and neighbouring states, to showcase Cuttack's maritime legacy, traditional art, handicrafts and rich cultural heritage.Baliyatra commemorates the glorious maritime history of ancient Kalinga, when Odia traders and sailors undertook voyages to Southeast Asian countries, including Bali, for trade and cultural exchanges. articles.summary: Delhi government to launch a mental well-being policy for children and youth up to age 25 on Nov 19, covering schools, colleges, and out-of-school groups.
articles.body: New Delhi: Delhi govt will launch its mental well-being policy on Nov 19, extending its outreach to people up to the age of 25 years.Education minister Ashish Sood Wednesday reviewed the proposed policy, which envisions an inclusive framework covering CM SHRI schools, govt and govt-aided schools, higher education institutions, private education institutions and children with special needs. articles.title: Day 2 of Yamuna cruise draws families, visitors seek more adventure options
articles.summary: Day 2 of Delhi’s Namo Yamuna River Cruise draws families; 236 riders. Visitors praise recreation but seek more adventure options and better facilities.
articles.body: New Delhi: Children took turns on swings, tried their hands at climbing a colourful tyre wall and bounced on a trampoline as several families Wednesday explored the cruise and recreational facilities launched by Delhi govt a day earlier.Near the musical fountain, groups gathered to watch the water jets while others headed towards the food court or waited to board the electric cruise. For many, the attraction was not just a ride on the Yamuna, but an opportunity to spend time outdoors with their families in a city with limited recreational options.The second day of the Namo Yamuna River Cruise Service saw 236 people take a ride and seven trying the jet ski facility. Families with children formed a significant part of the visitors. Gaurav and Shobha, who came with their family from Mukherjee Nagar, said, “We thought of coming because the river looks cleaner than before.”For Renu Gupta from Mandawali, the visit was an opportunity to give her three children an experience they had rarely had growing up in Delhi. articles.title: Trump wants a non-nuclear Iran. What’s the plan?
articles.summary: As President Trump maintains there is no rush to act against Iran, the administration faces internal debate over whether continued pressure will lead to a durable non-nuclear settlement.
articles.body:
President Trump says there is “no rush” to decide his next move against Iran.

That may sound prudent. After years of confrontation, many Americans would prefer patience to another military escalation. But waiting is not a neutral choice. Every additional week of pressure reflects a judgment that more time will produce something worth having.

Trump has been clear about the objective: a non-nuclear Iran. The unanswered question is how much additional pressure is expected to get us there, and what diplomatic settlement would make that outcome durable.

The debate after the election should therefore concern more than whether Trump orders another strike. It should focus on how American pressure becomes an achievable political settlement.

Reports suggest the debate inside the administration is not about the goal itself but about timing. Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff reportedly favor moving more quickly toward an agreement. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly favor giving pressure more time to work .

The most consequential argument appears to come from Ratcliffe. According to Axios, citing a source with direct knowledge of the discussions, he believes prolonged hardship could produce additional Iranian concessions or create enough instability to encourage political unrest. The CIA declined to comment.

That is a significant strategic wager. Washington should judge it by the commitments it helps secure, not simply by the hardship it imposes.

Supporters of patience deserve a fair hearing.

There are signs that pressure may be creating diplomatic opportunities. Qatari mediators have circulated a proposal aimed at restarting direct negotiations. Iranian officials have described intensified exchanges. Vance has said progress has been made.

On Nov. 5, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran would neither reopen the Strait of Hormuz nor negotiate until Washington met seven Iranian conditions. Reuters separately reported that Iran submitted a nuclear proposal through Qatar while making further discussions conditional on prior American concessions.

In other words, Tehran is still talking. It is also still demanding.

Neither fact proves that a workable agreement is within reach. Neither proves diplomacy has failed. The real question is whether both sides can identify a sequence of reciprocal steps that narrows the gap between them.

Pressure can strengthen a negotiating position and raise the costs of noncooperation. But hardship alone does not show that Iran’s leadership is becoming more willing, or more able, to accept American demands.

Just as important, concessions and political upheaval are not the same objective.

One requires authorities that can negotiate, implement and uphold commitments. The other creates uncertainty about who might be in charge tomorrow and whether any commitment would survive.

Washington does not need to disclose every detail of a negotiation. It does need to make the basic bargain understandable: What verifiable Iranian actions would trigger what reciprocal American steps?

While Washington debates whether to wait, other governments are moving.

During Sultan Haitham bin Tarik’s visit to Beijing this month, Oman and China called for renewed U.S.-Iran negotiations, safe navigation through Hormuz and a return to their earlier Islamabad memorandum of understanding. They also welcomed a larger Chinese role in regional security and stability.

A few days later, Rezaei traveled to Moscow and delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to Iranian state media.

Those meetings do not represent a diplomatic breakthrough. Nor do they prove that China and Russia are building an alternative peace process. They do show that other governments are looking for ways to shape the outcome while Washington weighs the benefits of continued pressure.

That could cut either way. Additional channels may reduce Tehran’s incentive to compromise with Washington. They could also help create opportunities for compromise by supplying mediators, technical expertise or verification arrangements.

The key question is not whether China or Russia participates. It is whether any outside involvement helps produce verifiable nuclear restrictions, safer shipping and a workable agreement.

Diplomacy should be judged by what it delivers, not by who receives the credit.

The Islamabad reference is also a reminder that negotiations are not starting from scratch. Washington should identify what remains unresolved and what additional gains it expects further pressure to secure.

The incoming Congress should make those questions central to its first review of Iran policy.

Jan. 3 offers a useful moment for accountability, not because diplomacy expires on that date, but because policymakers should be able to explain what their strategy has achieved.

Congress has already expressed opposition to continued hostilities. On June 23, the Senate adopted a House-passed concurrent resolution by a vote of 50 to 48 , though the measure was nonbinding. Another declaration alone would not answer the larger strategic question.

Instead, any request for additional funding to expand offensive operations should be accompanied by a public assessment of objectives, costs, negotiating gains and alternatives, supplemented by classified material where necessary.

That review should identify concrete indicators of progress: restored inspection access, credible accounting of nuclear materials, accepted monitoring arrangements or an agreed sequence linking Iranian actions to American relief.

It should distinguish commitments from implementation and weigh both against the military, economic and escalation risks of continuing the current course.

Any future settlement also needs clearly defined responsibilities. Verification, mediation, custody of nuclear material and enforcement are different functions. A workable agreement must establish who performs each role, how disputes are resolved and what consequences follow violations.

The administration does not need to prove that pressure caused every concession. It does need to explain why continued pressure offers a better path than the available alternatives.

Trump is right to insist on a non-nuclear Iran. But pressure is a means, not an end.

The administration is asking for more time. It should explain what more time is expected to deliver.

Charbel A. Antoun is a Washington-based journalist and writer specializing in U.S. foreign policy, with a focus on the Middle East and North Africa.

articles.title: Russia announces sudden death of ambassador to US
articles.summary: Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday announced the death of the country’s ambassador to the U.S., Alexander Darchiev. The diplomat died “suddenly” Nov. 11 at the age of 66, according to a statement shared by the Russian government on Telegram, which did not include a cause of death. The foreign ministry expressed “profound sorrow” at the…
articles.body:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday announced the death of the country’s ambassador to the U.S., Alexander Darchiev .

The diplomat died “suddenly” Nov. 11 at the age of 66, according to a statement shared by the Russian government on Telegram, which did not include a cause of death.

The foreign ministry expressed “profound sorrow” at the news of Darchiev’s death and called him an “outstanding diplomat.”

“An exceptional professional and a distinguished expert on the United States, Alexander Darchiev served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy,” the statement read.

“We extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Alexander Darchiev’s family and loved ones,” it continued. “The cherished memory of our colleague, taken from us far too soon, will remain in our hearts forever.”

Darchiev has served as the Russian ambassador to the U.S. since March 2025, after being appointed to the role by Russian President Vladimir Putin. He previously led his country’s North America Department and served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada for seven years.

In a statement posted to social media , the Russian embassy in Washington, D.C., said Darchiev “devoted his entire life to steadfastly defending Russian interests” and “building relations” with the U.S.

“Alexander Nikitich was distinguished by his trust in his subordinates and his deep respect for people,” the post read.

“He always sought to unite the staff and create a working environment in which the support of a senior, more experienced colleague was there to lean on whenever needed,” the statement continued. “We all repaid his warmth, kindness, and sincerity in kind.”
