articles.title: Complete data could've raised average Diwali pollution level 49%
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Missing PM2.5 data from monitoring stations could have raised the city's average pollution level by 49% on Diwali, according to an analysis by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Missing PM2.5 data from monitoring stations could have raised the city's average pollution level by 49% on Diwali, according to an analysis by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).Had the missing readings been recorded at 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (g/m³), the city's average PM2.5 level would have increased from 269 to 400(g/m³), it revealed. The daily national ambient air quality standard for PM2.5 is 60 g/m³ and WHO's safe guideline is 15 g/m³.The analysis was done a day after Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) said its stations' analysers were calibrated to measure particulate matter concentrations only up to 1,000g/m³ and could not display readings beyond it on Diwali night for several hours.Nor were these readings considered for calculating the average AQI, it said.CREA said if 400g/m³ had been considered, city's AQI on Monday would have risen from 344 (very poor) to near severe. AQI is calculated based on 8 pollutants, including PM2.5.TOI reported Tuesday that CPCB had stopped giving data on particulate matter at the peak of Diwali night pollution for several hours after particulate matter levels at air quality monitoring stations surpassed 1,000g/m³.However, Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which operates 43 of the total 60 stations, gave readings on Diwali night that crossed 1,000g/m³. At least at 11 locations, the hourly PM2.5 concentration was above 2,000g/m³. In four, it was above 3,000.CPCB compiles data from all 60 stations and releases the AQI. One station has been defunct for the past few months.The latest analysis examined hourly PM2.5 data from 59 monitoring stations between 4pm on Nov 8 and 4pm on Nov 9, corresponding to the 24-hour averaging period used for CPCB's 4pm AQI bulletin on Nov 9. It analysed 1,416 hours (24 hours x 59 stations).It found that 255 of the 1,416 expected station-hour observations or 18% were missing. CREA conducted a sensitivity analysis by assigning them a value of 1,000g/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB for particulate matter. Under this scenario, the pooled average PM2.5 concentration across the expected observations increased from 269g/m³ to 400g/m³, a rise of 49%."The peak PM2.5 levels of Delhi was 584 g/m³ at 1am on Nov 9 when there was missing data. However, after replacing the missing data with 1,000 g/m³, the peak PM2.5 concentration was 825 g/m³ at 2am and 824 g/m³ at 3am," said CREA.It clarified that the sensitivity analysis does not establish that all 255 missing observations were caused by PM2.5 concentrations exceeding 1,000g/m³. Assigning the upper measurement limit to these observations was only an illustrative exercise to understand how the reported average could change under such a scenario.TOI reported Tuesday that hourly PM2.5 levels at Mundka touched 3,744g/m³ at 2am Monday, according to DPCC's data. However, CPCB did not share Mundka's PM2.5 readings from 12 midnight to 4 am.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: NYC parents and locals protest homeless men's shelter being built a short walk from middle school
articles.summary: Canarsie residents erupted in protest Monday night over a 200-bed homeless men's shelter planning to be built one block from a Brooklyn middle school.
articles.body: Parents across Brooklyn's Canarsie neighborhood are demanding answers from New York City officials and Mayor Zohran Mamdani over plans to build a 200-bed men's homeless shelter just one block from a local middle school. Parents, teachers and other residents protested Monday night against plans for a 200-bed men's homeless shelter on East 108th Street that is expected to open in 2028, one block from the Science and Medicine Middle School 366 on East 107th Street. Among the protesters was New York City Council member Mercedes Narcisse, who represents the 46th District and criticized the city's Department of Social Services (DSS) in comments reported by News 12 Brooklyn. SEE IT: MASSIVE NYC HOMELESS ENCAMPMENT FUELS BACKLASH AGAINST MAMDANI "You want to put it next to a school — a middle school for God's sake! These are our children! Shame!" Narcisse said. Narcisse said DSS informed her about the proposed shelter last week but had not sought her input, even though she represents the neighborhood. According to News 12 Brooklyn, the upcoming shelter is part of a broader citywide plan to open 12 new shelters, including three in Brooklyn. PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION' Narcisse has requested a meeting with the DSS commissioner for Thursday to discuss residents' concerns. However, many protesters are calling for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to attend. "I asked for the commissioner, but now, my community says the mayor," Narcisse said. DSS confirmed plans to construct more shelters across the city and emphasized community engagement as part of the process. "Notifying elected officials and community boards is a part of the public process around siting new shelters. Notification is the beginning of a process that includes opportunity for community engagement," DSS told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital reached out to the Science and Medicine Middle School 366, Narcisse's office and Mamdani's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. articles.title: Ring of Honor champ Deonna Purrazzo bringing wrestling to NJ town to raise awareness about major issue
articles.summary: Deonna Purrazzo teams with Steve Maclin at Jefferson Township High School to spotlight New Jersey's S-2 funding formula crisis hitting Highlands schools.
articles.body: Ring of Honor women’s pure champion Deonna Purrazzo is set to return to her hometown in New Jersey to help raise money for her alma mater high school and raise awareness about the lack of funding for the schools in that area of the state. Purrazzo’s JTown SmackDown will take place at Jefferson Township High School in Oak Ridge on Friday night. The event means more than just teaming up with her husband, fellow pro wrestling star Steve Maclin. She is looking to put the spotlight on a serious issue that is near to her heart. "I've worked with the athletic director, Bill Koch, for the past few months, since earlier this year, really, when we were reconnected over the Highlands Impact Aid Now rally at Jefferson, where we're trying to draw attention to the fact that the funding formula for schools in New Jersey, the S-2 funding formula is not fair," Purrazzo told OutKick Dropkick. "It's not equitable to the students of the Highlands and the Pinelands. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE "And so that kind of was the precipice to JTown SmackDown. We were raising money for the athletic department and for the JTEF, the Jefferson Township Educational Fund, which is all going to the students." New Jersey’s S-2 funding formula was enacted as part of a revision to the 2008 School Funding Reform Act, which was meant to take aim at funding inadequacies across the state. But Purrazzo and other local officials have said it’s created a bigger issue for the township. Part of the issue, Purrazzo has said, is the Highlands Act. The piece of legislation protects hundreds of thousands acres of land in the Highlands, which is the main source of drinking water for millions of residents in New Jersey. The act comes with development restrictions, which critics have said hampers growth in places like Jefferson Township. "The S-2 funding formula and how it affects the Highlands is multifaceted. Fifteen or so years ago, there was a piece of legislation put in place in the Highlands that restricted the growth of the land in the tax base. And so, 88% of Jefferson Township is under this protection where new businesses can't come in, affordable housing can't be built, you can't rent out houses or build on your property because all of the land is protected. They provide millions and millions of gallons of water to all across New Jersey every single day. While environmental protection is important, it's limiting the growth of our students. "What's happened because of that is taxes have risen in town. We've lost the funding formula because people are moving out of town. Enrollment is how they equate funding for the schools. And so because our enrollments down, the funding goes down ... It's not been fair. Meanwhile, cities like Newark are able to build new buildings and hire new teachers and all these things that Jefferson Township and the surrounding towns are just not able to do. So, the awareness is coming from, we have to refigure out how this formula works, especially in these towns where the tax base isn't allowed to grow, and how do we make it equitable for these towns who literally can't up their enrollment." The New Jersey Education Association said last month it was taking on the task of rewriting the funding formula with the hope that it would be implemented during the 2027-28 school year. Jefferson Township Superintendent Jeanne Howe warned in March that the district could have to make cuts and increase classroom sizes if money doesn’t start to flow in, according to the Morristown Daily Record. In recent years, New Jersey lawmakers have worked together to provide millions of dollars to districts that saw reductions in funding because of the S-2 formula. Getting down to business Purrazzo hopes that a return to her high school would put the issue in a larger spotlight. She recalled speaking at one of the rallies earlier this year, which took place at the high school as well. "I don't know how I'm gonna react because when I was there in March for the Highlands Impact Aid rally, I spoke and I gave like a 7 or 8 minute speech about how growing up in this town really shaped my character for the rest of my life and allowed me to become a six-time world champion and travel the world as a professional wrestler, but they played my entrance music when I walked up to the podium and I started crying, which I didn't expect, right? " I was just overwhelmed with, there were so many familiar faces in the crowd, and obviously, it's for such a great cause. I'm getting a master's degree in political science, but I've never really stepped on a stage and spoken about policies and legislation, things that I was doing that day. So it was definitely a step out of my comfort zone, but really rewarding to be able to start there and now have worked through producing a wrestling show. I don't know exactly how I'm gonna feel. There might be a few tears, but it'll all be worth it." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Purrazzo and Maclin will take on VSK and Emily Jaye, Goldy will go up against Griffin McCoy Tiara James will square off against Tina San Antonio and Oxx Adams will face off against Marcus Mathers. Jaye is a highly talented young women’s wrestler who is among the next crop of talent that pro wrestling fans should pay attention to. She made her All Elite Wrestling debut earlier this year and has performed at several promotions from Gamechanger Wrestling to Boca Raton Championship Wrestling. Purrazzo said her advice to someone like Jaye is the same for any up-and-coming female star. "I say to her exactly what I say to all the women's wrestlers who are coming up right now: Don't quit on yourself," she told OutKick Dropkick. "There's going to be so many people who, for me, didn't know what ‘The Virtuosa’ meant, didn't see the vision in it, didn't understand that it's not this like overt in your face character. It is very nuanced, but it is very me, and I believed in it and I knew that if someone would give me the investment and the opportunity to educate the audience in terms of what that meant for me, it would click. And so, my biggest advice to Emily and all of the women coming up right now is, if you have a vision for yourself and you believe in it 100%, don't let anyone's opinions deter you. articles.title: Trump embraces Huang as espionage scandal shakes Nvidia
articles.summary: President Trump is standing by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the tech executive’s affair with an alleged spy, heightening national security concerns around the unfolding scandal. While tech observers and lawmakers said Trump’s quick defense of Huang was expected, the situation raises questions about Trump’s tight allyship with industry leaders, and whether it could undermine…
articles.body:
President Trump is standing by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the tech executive’s affair with an alleged spy, heightening national security concerns around the unfolding scandal.

While tech observers and lawmakers said Trump’s quick defense of Huang was expected, the situation raises questions about Trump’s tight allyship with industry leaders, and whether it could undermine their joint push for AI development in the United States.

“I think the president’s impulse was to quell markets, and you know he’s not the one running any investigation,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at Foundation for American Innovation, said of Trump’s response.

Huang admitted this week he was “unfaithful” to his wife and seemingly confirmed an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data center and cloud computing firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials concluded Alice Huang was recruited by China to pass along information.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang also had an extramarital affair with another executive at Nvidia. The Wall Street Journal later reported Wednesday evening that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang.

Trump on Sunday called the Nvidia CEO an “honorable guy,” telling reporters, “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”

“I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job and so I would certainly hope he’s a fine person, in my opinion,” he added.

The president later said Huang told him he was not aware the Megaspeed executive was an intelligence operative for Beijing.

“His defense of Mr. Huang so far doesn’t seem very full-throated,” Fedasiuk said. “He made a few comments saying that you know he’s a good guy and they have a good relationship, and I think that is within the realm of expectation.”

Over the past two years, Huang has become one of Trump’s closest allies in the tech space. When concerns around AI safety came to a head earlier this year, the Nvidia CEO was one of the only AI executives to stand behind the president’s push to continue full-steam ahead on development.

Huang has been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” on tech, and joined him on a summit to China last spring. In September, Haung was one of just a few executives chosen to sit with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the state dinner at the White House.

The Times first reported last month Trump was briefed about a year ago that the U.S. intelligence community believed Alice Huang was an operative for China’s government. The president didn’t do anything with the information at the time, according to the NYT, and even invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One when he flew to China in May.

But Trump said Monday that he found out about the issue with Huang “not too long ago.”

“Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago,” he said. “And we’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

The NYT reported this week the Commerce Department abruptly stopped its investigation into Megaspeed and passed it off to the Department of Justice.

The agency was investigating Megaspeed last year over suspicions the company was smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China, despite U.S. export controls. It stopped after concerns were raised around a Commerce official’s interactions with Nvidia’s general counsel, The Times reported.

The details of this report were not confirmed by either agency and the DOJ declined to comment.

Details are still unfolding, but national security experts are questioning whether Trump and Huang’s relationship presented new national security risks.

“Because Trump and Huang are so close, or apparently seem to be so close, did this Alice Huang character get access to information that would help inform China’s positioning via-a-vis the U.S. government?” Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, asked in an interview with The Hill.

“Did she learn details about how the Trump administration was thinking about U.S.-China competition, artificial intelligence policy, export controls?” he added.

The scrutiny has exploded on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are calling for investigations into whether Huang compromised national security and for the passage of chip export control bills.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) told CNBC on Wednesday: “I can’t believe we are even considering him not resigning. I mean, I do feel that strongly about it.”

Some Republicans defended Trump for his allyship with the CEO.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), who has clashed with Huang over export controls, said it would be “worse” if the U.S. “did not have a relationship” with Nvidia and its leader.

“If your president didn’t have that relationship … that would be a bad thing,” Mast told The Hill. “We want [Huang’s] relationship with the American president, not [Chinese President] Xi Jinping, as an example.”

“Do I worry about the president’s ability to make sure that he is cognizant of all national security concerns with his conversation? No I do not,” the Florida Republican added.

Fedasiuk also suggested it would be hard for the administration to separate itself from Nvidia.

“Nvidia is at the heart of the American AI buildout, and this technology sector is so essential to the American economy. And so it’s very difficult for the president of the United States to try to distance himself from the company so forcefully,” he said.

“I think…that the administration is taking this issue seriously, even if it is a difficult thing to fully distance the U.S. government from Nvidia.”

Mast was among a trio of GOP lawmakers who asked Huang last week to appear for a closed-door briefing about the company’s security protocols. He floated issuing a subpoena for Huang if he does not respond.

When asked whether they would accept an executive other than Huang to appear, Mast said, “We want to see Jensen here. He’s the one that was getting into bed with someone.”

articles.title: Father charged with attempted murder after baby survives being buried in crate
articles.summary: The father of an 11-month-old boy found alive after being buried in a dog crate has been charged with attempted murder and other counts, authorities said Wednesday.
articles.body: The father of an 11-month-old boy found alive after being buried in a dog crate has been charged with attempted murder and other counts, authorities said Wednesday. The baby, Koah Sharp, was allegedly taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, on Monday and the child was dug out of the ground Tuesday afternoon, the Lexington County, South Carolina, sheriff said. The baby is expected to make a full recovery. He is believed to have been buried in the wire crate, which was wrapped in a towel for around 24 hours, Sheriff Brayn “Jay” Koon said. The towel likely created an air pocket that allowed the Koah to breathe, and cool weather may have also helped the child to survive, Koon said. Comer, who was arrested on a burglary charge after being found in an outbuilding Monday night, is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary, the sheriff’s office said Wednesday. Searchers investigating a patch of disturbed earth near a home owned by Comer’s father heard the baby’s cries and quickly unearthed him, Koon said. Koah was released from the hospital Tuesday, the sheriff’s office said, and the child is with family members. The child was reported missing early Monday afternoon, authorities said. The report set off a search for the infant that included the FBI, firefighters, the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and local law enforcement agencies. Comer was in custody Wednesday, jail records showed. It was not immediately clear whether he had an attorney who could speak on his behalf. Koah’s mother has custody of the child, Comer’s mother has said. The child’s mother told a sheriff’s deputy that she allowed Comer to briefly have the child but only expected that to last a day or two, according to a police report. The mother told the deputy that Comer had threatened her over Facebook Messenger that he would keep the baby, according to the police report.

articles.title: US election results could be positive for Lebanon, Hezbollah chief says
articles.summary: Naim Qassem says Republican losses and Israel’s election result could help Lebanon maintain sovereignty.
articles.body:
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has welcomed Republican setbacks in US midterm elections last week and a lacklustre showing for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli polls, calling them a boon for Lebanon.

During a speech on Wednesday honouring members of the group killed by Israel, along with their families, Qassem described the elections in the US as an “earthquake” and the Israeli elections as a “defeat”. The bloc of Netanyahu, an arch-nemesis of the group, fell short of the 61 seats it needed to stay in power after the October 27 vote.

Qassem said the results were good for Lebanon and a signal that the country should resist the Trump administration’s push to disarm the group.

“Come, let us rebuild our country together, save it from the darkness of failure, and protect it from the empty rhetoric of those who sow discord and those who rely on American tutelage,” he said in a video-link address.

“Lebanon belongs to all of us. We are partners in building it and sharing the cost of protecting its sovereignty.”

Iran-backed Hezbollah is locked in a standoff with US-backed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun over whether it will relinquish its arms, in a move Washington seeks but the group says would be a surrender to Israel.

The Hezbollah leader insisted it would not hand over its weapons and cited a continued Israeli military occupation over parts of the country’s south.

“There will be no state monopoly on the resistance’s weapons, no regulation, no prohibition, and no disarmament under Israeli occupation,” Qassem said.

The secretary-general assumed the role after Israel assassinated former Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah and his successor Hashem Safieddine in 2024.

Sparking months of ongoing war, the US and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran in February, assassinating Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah’s retaliation by firing missiles and drones into Israel led to weeks of intense Israeli strikes on south Lebanon, in which more than 4,300 people were killed, Lebanese authorities say, and around a million were displaced, according to the United Nations.

Qassem praised Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz for causing a spike in global oil prices and suspending shipping routes, saying it would weaken American and Israeli influence in the region.

US President Donald Trump has also acknowledged the role of the Iran war and the rise in fuel prices it stoked in last week’s electoral drubbing for Republicans, as did US Vice President and likely 2028 electoral hopeful JD Vance.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance said last week.

Qassem also warned against Lebanese authorities making commitments and deals that serve Israeli goals and urged them to focus on domestic issues.

“Why are you binding yourselves before the world to positions that serve the Israeli project?” he asked.

Israel continues to occupy large swathes of southern Lebanon and has decimated dozens of the roughly 60 villages and towns it occupies.

Although Israel and Lebanon negotiated a ceasefire with US mediation in June, Israel continues to bomb south Lebanon.

articles.title: Rachel Maddow welcomes 'big fight' between socialist and moderate Democrats after midterm wins
articles.summary: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow told "The View" she hopes moderate Democrats and democratic socialists have a "big fight" that strengthens the party's big tent.
articles.body: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow told ABC's "The View" Wednesday she hopes there will be a "big fight" between moderate and socialist members of the Democratic Party in Congress. While promoting her new book "Department of Fate," Maddow discussed recent calls from some progressive senators to replace Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., once Democrats take control of the Senate in January. Those calling for new leadership included Democratic senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER Though some Democrats have expressed concerns about infighting within the party, Maddow dismissed those concerns and welcomed the idea of moderate Democrats debating socialists. "I feel like the Democrats have kind of first-world problems right now," Maddow joked. "There was so much talk ahead of the election about, ‘Oh there’s these handful of democratic socialist-associated candidates. How are the Democrats going to do?’ "Well, the Democrats elected so many people. Yes, they elected a handful of democratic socialists, but also the Blue Dog coalition, which is the conservative Democrats. They have like a dozen new members too." Maddow argued that the Democratic Party now includes members with a wide range of political views and that debate could strengthen the party. "I think that it’s righteous for them to have a big fight. I hope they don’t settle it instantly. I hope they actually do have a debate. I think competition makes us stronger," she said. Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. BILL MAHER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT SOME ON FAR LEFT WANT 'COMMUNISM' AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP Maddow's comments came one day after "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg called out congressional Democrats publicly debating whether to replace Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as party leaders. "This is my two cents," Goldberg said. "I don’t want to hear this from you right now. I want to know what all of you are, all of you Democrats, what are your plans for the first 100 days? I don’t care if you’ve been there forever or just got there. What are your plans? "We put you in there to clean house, to make sure that the government works the way the people want it to work," she added. "I don’t want to hear all this infighting, because then you become the distraction, and then you become no better than the Republicans were. So, just get your stuff together. All of you." MADDOW FEARS TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION CENTERS MAY BE USED TO IMPRISON ‘THE REST OF US’ Democratic strategist and pollster Doug Schoen disagreed with Maddow's assessment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s clear the Dems won an overwhelming victory because of moderates, not progressives. The American people are demanding action on the affordability crisis, not intraparty infighting between progressives and moderates," Schoen told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free status
articles.summary: An independent commission is reviewing whether countries in the Americas still meet measles elimination criteria.
articles.body:
International health experts are meeting in Washington, DC, this week to determine which countries in the Americas have endemic measles transmission.

The outcome could decide whether the United States, Mexico and Guatemala retain their “measles elimination status”: a designation that the virus has not spread uncontrolled domestically for at least 12 months.

The Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (RVC) began its annual conference on Tuesday to assess the countries’ status. The conference will adjourn on Friday.

The review comes as a sharp resurgence of the virus has spread across the Americas, with the US experiencing its largest and deadliest measles outbreak in nearly 30 years. The US has held its elimination status since 2000, but it risks losing it this year.

The commission will review reports submitted by all 35 PAHO member states, with particular attention to countries experiencing prolonged outbreaks.

How does the process work? Al Jazeera breaks down what happens in this explainer.

Who decides whether a country has eliminated measles?

The RVC is an independent panel of international experts in epidemiology, public health and virology. The group advises PAHO, which is part of the World Health Organization, on which countries have maintained the elimination of measles and rubella.

The Americas became the first region in the world to eliminate endemic measles transmission in 2016, following decades of vaccination campaigns. For this year’s review, the commission is examining epidemiological data from 2025 and the first half of 2026.

Which countries could lose their elimination status this year?

The US, Mexico, Guatemala, Peru and Bolivia are at risk. Canada lost its status last November.

The US, which eliminated endemic measles transmission in 2000, has experienced sustained outbreaks since January 2025. Mexico has also reported prolonged transmission.

PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed measles cases across 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and October 2026.

Experts at the conference evaluate whether infections result from separate introductions of the virus or whether the same strain has circulated locally.

Reported measles cases or deaths alone do not determine whether a country loses its elimination status. Some cases, for instance, come from exposure to measles during travel. A limited outbreak due to such exposure would not result in the loss of a country’s measles elimination status.

Under PAHO’s criteria, a country loses its elimination status if the same measles virus strain continues to spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months in a country or defined geographical area.

Investigators use genetic sequencing to determine whether infections are linked to the same virus strain. They also examine epidemiological data to establish how the virus has spread and whether transmission has been interrupted.

In addition, the commission considers vaccination coverage, how healthcare systems monitor measles cases, and the speed of outbreak responses in its decisions.

The commission’s deliberations in Washington run until Friday. It will assess the evidence and make recommendations on the status of individual countries to PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa, who will make the final determination.

The official announcement is expected early next week following the conclusion of the conference.

What happens if the US loses its status?

Experts agree that the US will likely lose its measles elimination status, marking a reversal of a major public-health achievement.

“It would be a disappointment, not a shock,” Matt Ferrari, the director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, told Al Jazeera. “This is moving backwards from a great public health achievement, and to see that backslide is just heart-wrenching.”

Although the loss of status would not trigger any immediate consequences, those working in the field say it would be an embarrassment.

“It’s a stain on your health programme,” Edwin Asturias, a professor of infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, told Al Jazeera.

The long-term effects include greater pressure on public-health systems, which must devote resources to identifying infections, tracing contacts, conducting laboratory tests, isolating patients and organising vaccination campaigns.

When asked about how a country generally responds to losing its measles elimination status, Asturias pointed to Brazil , which found itself in that predicament in 2019. The country regained its measles-free designation in 2024 after launching a strategic vaccination campaign. But Asturias does not believe that the US will mount a similarly robust response.

On Tuesday, Erica Schwartz , the director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said losing elimination status would not change the agency’s approach to measles.

“Let’s say we did lose our measles elimination status. We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” Schwartz told the news agency Reuters.

Ferrari said the announcement could nonetheless galvanise action at state and local levels by giving public-health officials and advocates shared language.

“Think globally, act locally,” Ferrari said. “We all will have the same language to talk about what’s going on. And that’s surprisingly important.”

articles.title: Bola Tinubu's manifesto: Can Nigeria's president deliver economic relief in a second term?
articles.summary: For Nigerians to feel meaningful improvements, reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined, analysts say.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.

The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.

Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.

Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.

The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.

The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.

"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.

"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.

Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.

In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.

However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.

"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.

The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.

Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.

Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.

However, he has recently said he will work to reduce fuel cost.

His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.

Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.

"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.

However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.

"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.

While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.

Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.

"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.

To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.

But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.

Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.

"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."

To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.

"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.

Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.

He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.

"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.

Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.

"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Nigeria's power sector has suffered from years of underinvestment. The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.

Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.

The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.

"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.

Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.

The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.

For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.

"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.

"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.

Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.

"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.

As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge: building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.

"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.

"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."
